question: How does file-based routing work in the App Router? What are layouts?
shortAnswer: Folders map to URL segments; page.tsx makes a route public. layout.tsx wraps its segment and all children, persists across navigations, and nests — a root layout holds <html>; nested layouts compose for shared section chrome.
explanation: The app directory encodes structure: app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx serves /dashboard/settings. Files have reserved meanings — page.tsx (route UI), layout.tsx (persistent wrapper), loading.tsx (Suspense fallback), error.tsx (error boundary), not-found.tsx, route.ts (API handler), template.tsx (layout that re-mounts on navigation). Layouts receive children and render them without unmounting during child navigation: state inside a sidebar survives moving between pages. Nesting composes naturally — root layout defines html/body; a dashboard layout adds nav; each page fills the innermost slot. Only one active page renders per URL; multiple layouts stack automatically. Route groups (folder-name) organize without affecting URLs, handy for marketing vs app shells with different roots. Colocation keeps private files beside their routes since only special filenames become endpoints.
interviewTip: Sketch the folder tree verbally while explaining layout persistence — the sidebar-stays-mounted example demonstrates you understand why layouts exist.
commonMistakes: Not knowing only special filenames create routes.
Confusing layouts with templates (templates remount per navigation).

question: How do dynamic routes work, and what does generateStaticParams do?
shortAnswer: [param] folders match dynamic segments, [...slug] catches rest, [[slug]] is optional catch-all. generateStaticParams pre-renders known param values at build time (SSG); unknown params either render on demand or 404 depending on dynamicParams.
explanation: Dynamic segments make data-driven URLs type-safe-ish: app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx receives params.slug. Catch-all [...slug] matches /docs/a/b/c; optional catch-all [[...slug]] also matches the bare prefix. In Server Components params arrives as a prop (a Promise in recent versions). generateStaticParams returns the list of values to prerender at build — like getStaticPaths before it — commonly fetching all slugs from your CMS or DB: return posts.map(p => ({ slug: p.slug })). The companion flag dynamicParams controls strangers: true (default) renders unknown params on demand then caches; false hard-404s anything not prerendered. Combine with revalidate for ISR on dynamic pages. Nested dynamics compose — parent and child each declare their own params. Common production concern: thousands of params × long builds → prefer on-demand rendering with caching over exhaustive prerendering.
interviewTip: Name all three segment syntaxes quickly, then focus on the generateStaticParams + dynamicParams pairing — that's where understanding actually shows.
commonMistakes: Not knowing dynamicParams controls whether unknown paths render.

question: What are Route Handlers and how do they replace API routes?
shortAnswer: Route Handlers live in route.ts files and export functions per HTTP method (GET, POST...), replacing pages/api/*. They're full Request/Response Web-standard handlers, cacheable like fetches, and colocated with the routes they serve.
explanation: app/api/users/route.ts exports async GET(request) { ... } replacing the old default-export switch statements. They use Web standard APIs — Request, Response, URLSearchParams — so code ports to edge runtimes, workers, tests unchanged. Method exports map directly to verbs; unsupported methods fall through to 405 automatically. Caching integrates with the same machinery as fetch: static handlers (no request-time input) can be prerendered, revalidate applies, dynamic = 'force-dynamic' forces runtime. Reading request data via searchParams/headers opts into dynamism. Handlers suit external API surface areas — webhooks, REST endpoints for mobile apps. Important nuance: when both client and server are Next.js, Server Components often call databases/services *directly*, skipping an internal API hop entirely — handlers aren't always needed. Middleware remains separate at the root for cross-cutting concerns.
interviewTip: Show the method-export mapping in code, then drop the senior insight — 'internal calls often skip HTTP entirely with RSC' — it reframes when handlers are actually necessary.
commonMistakes: Building internal APIs out of habit instead of querying from Server Components.
Not knowing Web-standard Request/Response powers them.

question: What is Next.js middleware and what do you use it for?
shortAnswer: middleware.ts runs before every matching request at the edge — rewriting URLs, redirecting, setting headers, and gating access by cookies. It can't run heavy logic or use Node APIs; think fast routing decisions, not business logic.
explanation: A single middleware.ts at the project root exports a function receiving every incoming request (filtered by matcher config): auth gates checking session cookies before protected routes render, A/B experiments rewriting to variant pages transparently, geo/locale redirects from headers, adding security headers globally, logging. It runs in a lightweight edge runtime: Web APIs yes, heavy Node libraries no, execution time budgeted in milliseconds. Two response patterns: NextResponse.next() passes through (optionally rewriting/adding headers), redirect()/rewrite() change destination. Rewrites differ from redirects — URL stays in browser while content swaps, enabling clean experiments. Matcher config limits scope cheaply ('/dashboard/:path*'). Common mistake: treating middleware as general backend code — DB queries and sessions belong in Server Components/handlers; middleware should decide *where* requests go, quickly.
interviewTip: List three concrete uses fast (auth gate, rewrites for experiments, header injection), then state the constraint that shapes design: edge runtime, milliseconds, no heavy compute.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the matcher config and running on every asset request.

question: How do loading.tsx, error.tsx and not-found.tsx work together?
shortAnswer: They're per-segment conventions built on React primitives: loading.tsx is an automatic Suspense boundary, error.tsx is an error boundary that must be a client component receiving reset(), not-found.tsx renders for 404s including notFound() calls. Each scopes to its folder level and nests.
explanation: Next.js turns common UI states into file conventions wrapping each route segment. loading.tsx wraps the segment's page in <Suspense fallback={<Loading/>}>: navigation shows it instantly while server data streams in — no manual skeleton wiring. error.tsx creates an Error Boundary catching render/data failures below its position; it must start with 'use client', receives error plus reset() to retry the segment without reloading the whole app — pair with a button calling reset(). not-found.tsx handles two triggers: users hitting unmatched URLs and code calling notFound() deliberately for missing records (the idiomatic 404 for dynamic params). Nesting means granular recovery: a failing widget errors its nearest boundary, keeping surrounding chrome alive. template.tsx rounds out the family (remounts on navigation). Together they encode resilient UI architecture declaratively.
interviewTip: Map each file to its React primitive (Suspense, ErrorBoundary) first — then the reset() retry flow and notFound() usage show practical fluency.
commonMistakes: Expecting error boundaries to catch event handlers or server actions.

question: What do route groups and underscore-prefixed folders do?
shortAnswer: (group) folders organize routes without affecting the URL — useful for different layout shells sharing a path space. Underscore prefixes mark private folders excluded from routing: _components, _lib keep colocation tidy.
explanation: Route groups wrap related routes in parentheses: app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx still serves /about but inherits only (marketing)/layout.tsx — letting marketing pages use one shell while app/(shop)/products uses another, even coexisting at the same URL path level (only one may claim a given final path though). Groups solve real problems: separate root layouts for auth flows, applying Suspense/loading per section, organizing without polluting URLs. Private folders (_name) opt files out of the filesystem router entirely — components, utilities, fixtures sit next to the routes using them without creating accidental endpoints; the alternative $ prefix opts back INTO routing for unusual needs. Conflicts to watch: groups sharing a path must not define competing pages at identical URLs, and multiple root layouts require groups with each holding its own html/body. These features reward deliberate information architecture.
example:
app/
├─ (marketing)/
│  ├─ layout.tsx        # marketing shell
│  └─ about/page.tsx    # /about
├─ (shop)/
│  ├─ layout.tsx        # shop shell w/ cart
│  └─ products/page.tsx # /products
└─ dashboard/
   ├─ _components/Chart.tsx   # NOT a route
   └─ page.tsx                # /dashboard
interviewTip: Draw the tree with both groups showing same-level URLs mapping to different layouts. The 'private folders prevent accidental routes' point shows attention to safety.
commonMistakes: Creating duplicate paths across groups causing build conflicts.
Not knowing _folders stay out of the router.

question: How does navigation work — Link vs router.push — and what does prefetching do?
shortAnswer: <Link> is the default: client-side transitions, prefetching viewport-visible routes, preserving scroll/state of shared layouts. router.push programmatically navigates (after mutations). Prefetching downloads route payloads ahead of clicks making transitions instant.
explanation: Link renders an anchor (SEO-friendly, middle-click works) but intercepts clicks for soft navigation: only changed segments fetch/render, layouts stay mounted, browser history updates correctly. Prefetching starts automatically when links scroll into viewport — static routes fully prefetch; dynamic ones fetch the shared layout/shell, streaming the rest on click. That's why App Router navigations feel instant. router.push/replace/back/refresh handle imperative cases: navigating after form success, programmatic redirects post-login, forcing refresh after mutations (router.refresh() re-fetches server components preserving client state — the idiomatic post-mutation update alongside revalidation). usePathname/useSearchParams power active-link styling and query-driven UI. Pitfalls: plain <a> tags lose prefetching and trigger full reloads; prefetch={false} disables eager fetching for logout links etc.; nested same-route push needs care to avoid duplicate history entries.
interviewTip: Explain prefetching behavior (viewport-triggered, static vs dynamic difference) — most candidates know Link but not how prefetching changes perceived performance.
commonMistakes: Using raw <a> tags internally, losing client navigation.
Not knowing router.refresh() exists for post-mutation server updates.
